lecture_beats.subject: The Black Hole War comic opening and brief commercial aside.
Alice and Bob return as the route back into group theory.
Audience asks how an abstract group differs from its concrete action.
A rotation is treated first as an abstract operation.
Physical quantities furnish objects on which rotations act.
Classical vectors and coordinate descriptions provide the first examples.
Quantum states live in vector spaces carrying group actions.
Representation dimension is counted by mutually orthogonal states.
One electron spin has a two-dimensional spin state space.
Two spins have four basis states.
Orbital wavefunctions furnish an infinite-dimensional space.
Rotations can therefore have infinite-dimensional representations.
Spin one-half uses two-by-two matrices.
Spin one uses three-by-three matrices.
Spin zero carries the trivial representation.
The spin-j sequence supplies representations of increasing dimension.
The same abstract group has many inequivalent representations.
Spinor rotations are represented by unitary matrices.
The representation law preserves group multiplication.
The inverse of a unitary matrix is its Hermitian conjugate.
A complex two-by-two matrix starts with eight real parameters.
Spatial rotations have only three continuous parameters.
The determinant-one condition removes the extra phase.
Determinants multiply under matrix products.
The determinant of the Hermitian conjugate is complex conjugated.
Unitarity constrains the determinant to unit modulus.
Determinant-one matrices close under multiplication.
Audience asks whether a unit-modulus determinant is still an arbitrary phase.
The common phase can be removed to isolate the special-unitary part.
SU(2) double-covers SO(3).
Continuous transformations are built from infinitesimal generators.
Finite transformations arise from repeated small steps.
Generators appear physically as conserved quantities.
The generator construction extends from SU(2) to SU(N).
A matrix close to the identity is expanded to first order.
First-order unitarity constrains the generator.
With the conventional factor of i, the generator is Hermitian.
Hermitian generators are observables.
SU(2) has three independent generator directions.
The determinant constraint is imposed infinitesimally.
The near-identity determinant exposes the trace.
Special unitarity requires a traceless generator.
Angular momentum operators generate rotations.
Generator commutators encode the local group structure.
Audience connects the generators to Pauli and Gell-Mann matrices.
Audience connects the eightfold way and eight gluons to SU(3).
The discussion passes from SU(2) to SU(3).
Parameter counting gives eighteen minus nine minus one equals eight.
Representations can be combined by tensor products.
Two spin one-half systems produce four states.
Those four states decompose into a singlet and triplet.
Hydrogen supplies the physical spin-coupling example.
The analogous SU(3) representations are introduced.
A quark transforms as a color triplet.
A color state is a coherent red-green-blue superposition.
The fundamental representation is denoted bold three.
An antiquark transforms in the conjugate representation.
Complex conjugation gives the anti-triplet action.
The anti-triplet is denoted three-bar.
U(1) charge conjugation provides a simple analogy.
Audience asks why the SU(2) doublet behaves differently under conjugation.
For SU(3), three and three-bar are inequivalent.
Anti-triplet generators carry the conjugate/opposite color action.
The product of two quark triplets is considered.
Three times three contains nine states.
The product decomposes as three-bar plus six.
Antisymmetric and symmetric color pairs realize those pieces.
A quark-antiquark product is then considered.
Three times three-bar contains a singlet.
The remaining states form an octet.
The octet is the adjoint representation associated with the generators.
Three-quark products are assembled.
The three-bar branch gives a singlet plus octet.
The six branch combines with a third triplet.
The color singlet is identified as physically central.
The RGB baryon color state is fully antisymmetric.
Audience asks about probabilities and energies of nonsinglet states.
Gluons are introduced as color-field quanta.
Gluons transform as a color octet.
Quarks, antiquarks, and gluons receive their QCD representations.
Audience asks why there is no additional color-singlet gluon.
Only color singlets appear as free finite-energy particles.
The elementary ways of building singlets are enumerated.
Audience asks how baryons, mesons, and glueballs fit the singlet rule.
The product of two gluon octets is considered.
The two-gluon state count is corrected to sixty-four.
Glueballs arise from color-singlet gluon combinations.
The hadron spectrum is organized by color-singlet composition.
Observed hadrons have integral electric charge.
Audience asks about the strange-quark charge assignment.
Quark flavors and their charge families are reviewed.
Audience identifies the baryon singlet as an entangled color state.
Audience asks what the tensor-product equations mean operationally.
Two-spin operators make the product representation explicit.
Tensor indices track the separate factors.
The product representation acts through four-by-four matrices.
The antisymmetric two-spin state is the singlet.
The symmetric states form the triplet.
The same decomposition logic is transferred to color.
Audience asks why arbitrary dimensions such as two plus seven are not allowed.
Allowed SU(3) irreducible dimensions are constrained by the group.
Neutrality analogies clarify the special status of singlets.
Audience asks for the explicit three-quark singlet.
The invariant epsilon tensor constructs the antisymmetric singlet.
The SU(3) epsilon tensor is written in color indices.
Audience requests the full eight-times-eight decomposition.
Each sector of the octet product is interpreted.
Audience requests the full three-quark decomposition.
Audience asks how the direct-sum sectors appear as matrix blocks.
Audience asks for the name of an invariant component.
Audience asks whether nonsinglet representations exist despite confinement.
Nambu's historical role in introducing color is recalled.
Fractional electric charge motivated the color construction.
The gluon-photon analogy is established.
Eight color charges source eight gluon fields.
A colored object is surrounded by a non-Abelian gluon field.
Separating charge and anticharge stores field energy.
Field-line energy gives the confinement intuition.
The strong coupling controls the importance of gluon self-interaction.
Nambu's large-color-coupling picture is developed.
Unlike the photon, a gluon itself carries color.
Photon linearity is contrasted with gluon self-interaction.
The nonlinear gluon field is pictured qualitatively.
A quark acts as a source of color flux.
Gluon self-interaction causes color flux to attract itself.
The flux bundles into tubes.
A quark-antiquark pair is connected by a color-flux tube.
The tube interior has approximately uniform field strength and energy density.
Flux-tube energy grows linearly with separation.
The tube is compared with a fluxoid.
An isolated nonsinglet would require infinite energy.
A struck quark cannot escape as a free colored particle.
Audience asks what happens when the string is stretched far enough.
Quark-antiquark pair creation breaks the string.
The broken string becomes two mesons.
Repeated string breaking produces jets of hadrons.
Audience asks how other hadrons fit the flux-tube picture.
A baryon is represented by a three-pronged flux junction.
The working meaning of gauge theory is introduced.
Continuous symmetry implies conserved charge.
Charge conservation is related to conserved flux.
Field lines can end only on charges.
Causality motivates local charge conservation.
Gauge-field sources must be conserved.
Nine of the Standard Model's twelve generators have been encountered.
SU(3), SU(2), and U(1) bookkeeping is laid out.
The Higgs mechanism is announced as the next topic.
The lecture closes with the CERN and beyond-Standard-Model roadmap.
